claim: The fly proboscis is a segmented appendage homologous to a limb.
source: Here we investigate the fly proboscis (mouthparts), a segmented appendage homologous to a limb (Bridges and Dobzhansky, 1933).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bridges and Dobzhansky, 1933

claim: The proboscis is capable of directed reaching towards a specifically placed food target, using gustatory information from taste receptors on the legs.
source: The proboscis is capable of directed reaching towards a specifically placed food target, using gustatory information from taste receptors on the legs as they move and contact food (Dethier, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dethier, 1976

claim: The proboscis extends during courtship.
source: Besides feeding, the proboscis also extends during courtship (Sturtevant, 1915), grooming (Szebenyi, 1969), flight-associated respiration (Lehmann and Heymann, 2005), and wing expansion after eclosion (Baker and Truman, 2002), suggesting that it is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sturtevant, 1915

claim: The proboscis extends during grooming.
source: Besides feeding, the proboscis also extends during courtship (Sturtevant, 1915), grooming (Szebenyi, 1969), flight-associated respiration (Lehmann and Heymann, 2005), and wing expansion after eclosion (Baker and Truman, 2002), suggesting that it is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
evidence: Supported by citation to Szebenyi, 1969

claim: The proboscis extends during flight-associated respiration.
source: Besides feeding, the proboscis also extends during courtship (Sturtevant, 1915), grooming (Szebenyi, 1969), flight-associated respiration (Lehmann and Heymann, 2005), and wing expansion after eclosion (Baker and Truman, 2002), suggesting that it is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lehmann and Heymann, 2005

claim: The proboscis extends during wing expansion after eclosion.
source: Besides feeding, the proboscis also extends during courtship (Sturtevant, 1915), grooming (Szebenyi, 1969), flight-associated respiration (Lehmann and Heymann, 2005), and wing expansion after eclosion (Baker and Truman, 2002), suggesting that it is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker and Truman, 2002

claim: The proboscis is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
source: Besides feeding, the proboscis also extends during courtship (Sturtevant, 1915), grooming (Szebenyi, 1969), flight-associated respiration (Lehmann and Heymann, 2005), and wing expansion after eclosion (Baker and Truman, 2002), suggesting that it is a multifunctional appendage that can be employed flexibly.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple contexts in which the proboscis extends

claim: In adult flies, most muscles are innervated by only one or a few motor neurons.
source: In adult flies, most muscles are innervated by only one or a few motor neurons (see, for example, Baek and Mann, 2009; O'Sullivan et al., 2018; Rajashekhar and Singh, 1994; Trimarchi and Schneiderman, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baek and Mann, 2009; O'Sullivan et al., 2018; Rajashekhar and Singh, 1994; Trimarchi and Schneiderman, 1994

claim: Previous efforts using GAL4 lines with broader expression patterns, or stochastic techniques to refine GAL4 lines, identified some of the critical motor neurons.
source: Previous efforts using GAL4 lines with broader expression patterns, or stochastic techniques to refine GAL4 lines, identified some of the critical motor neurons (Gordon and Scott, 2009; Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon and Scott, 2009; Schwarz et al., 2017

claim: The split GAL4 technique intersects two expression patterns to genetically target only the cells in common between the two.
source: Here we use the split GAL4 technique, which intersects two expression patterns to genetically target only the cells in common between the two (Luan et al., 2006), to provide more precise and reproducible targeting of particular neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Luan et al., 2006

claim: A collection of split GAL4 fly strains was created to identify and separately target the primary motor neurons for every proboscis muscle.
source: We create a collection of split GAL4 fly strains to identify and separately target the primary motor neurons for every proboscis muscle.
evidence: Described as a result of the study

claim: 8 of the 16 proboscis muscles are predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning.
source: We predict that 8 of the 16 proboscis muscles should be involved in proboscis positioning (such as reaching), and the other half should be involved in the proboscis' other main function, pumping food through the pharynx (investigated by others; Flood et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998).
evidence: Prediction based on anatomical analysis and supported by citations to previous work on pharyngeal pumping

claim: 8 of the 16 proboscis muscles are predicted to be involved in pumping food through the pharynx.
source: We predict that 8 of the 16 proboscis muscles should be involved in proboscis positioning (such as reaching), and the other half should be involved in the proboscis' other main function, pumping food through the pharynx (investigated by others; Flood et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998).
evidence: Prediction based on anatomical analysis and supported by citations to Flood et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998

claim: The proboscis is extended during feeding.
source: Work that predated confocal microscopy (Miller, 1950) showed that the proboscis is extended during feeding.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1950

claim: Food is sucked in through the lip-like labella at the tip of the proboscis.
source: Work that predated confocal microscopy (Miller, 1950) showed that the proboscis is extended during feeding. Food is sucked in through the lip-like labella at the tip, then pumped through the pharynx, traveling through two segments of the proboscis, first the haustellum then the rostrum.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1950

claim: Food is pumped through the pharynx, traveling through the haustellum then the rostrum.
source: Food is sucked in through the lip-like labella at the tip, then pumped through the pharynx, traveling through two segments of the proboscis, first the haustellum then the rostrum.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1950 in the preceding sentence

claim: Inside the head, food enters the esophagus, which passes through a foramen in the brain.
source: Inside the head, food then enters the esophagus, which passes through a foramen in the brain, and carries food towards the gut.
evidence: Anatomical description based on imaging shown in Figure 1A

claim: In the retracted state, the rostrum rests near the brain inside the head, and the haustellum is folded up against the rostrum.
source: In the retracted state, the rostrum rests near the brain inside the head, and the haustellum is folded up against the rostrum (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A

claim: When the rostrum extends, it is protracted ventrally out of the head capsule.
source: When the rostrum extends, it is protracted ventrally out of the head capsule.
evidence: Anatomical observation from imaging

claim: The outer cuticle of the rostrum is largely unsclerotized, giving it flexibility to fold like skin.
source: The outer cuticle of the rostrum is largely unsclerotized, giving it flexibility to fold like skin; support for several muscles therefore comes from an internal skeleton of rigid cuticular structures (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Anatomical observation from imaging shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: Support for several muscles comes from an internal skeleton of rigid cuticular structures.
source: The outer cuticle of the rostrum is largely unsclerotized, giving it flexibility to fold like skin; support for several muscles therefore comes from an internal skeleton of rigid cuticular structures (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Anatomical observation from imaging shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: The haustellum extends and flexes from its joint with the rostrum.
source: The haustellum extends and flexes from its joint with the rostrum.
evidence: Anatomical observation from imaging and video

claim: The rostrum pivots around a point on the anterior head designated the rostrum joint.
source: Gluing the head and one proboscis joint shows only the movement of the remaining joint: the rostrum pivots around a point on the anterior head that we designate the rostrum joint (Video 3, and also visible in Video 1), and the haustellum pivots around a point near the rostrum-haustellum junction (Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by gluing experiments shown in Videos 1, 3, and 4

claim: The haustellum pivots around a point near the rostrum-haustellum junction.
source: Gluing the head and one proboscis joint shows only the movement of the remaining joint: the rostrum pivots around a point on the anterior head that we designate the rostrum joint (Video 3, and also visible in Video 1), and the haustellum pivots around a point near the rostrum-haustellum junction (Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by gluing experiments shown in Video 4

claim: For a freely moving fly to feed, the proboscis must extend ventrally if the food is on the surface on which the fly is standing.
source: We had observed that, for a freely moving fly to feed, the proboscis must extend ventrally if the food is on the surface on which the fly is standing (Figure 2A, Video 5).
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2A and Video 5

claim: A male courting a female on a flat surface typically extends his proboscis anteriorly towards the female for courtship licking.
source: In contrast, we find that a male courting a female on a flat surface typically extends his proboscis anteriorly towards the female for courtship licking (Figure 2B, Video 6).
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2B and Video 6

claim: Both the head and the rostrum were angled higher (more anteriorly) in courtship experiments than in feeding.
source: Both the head and the rostrum were angled higher (more anteriorly) in the courtship experiments than in feeding, on average (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2E-F

claim: The haustellum was more extended for ventral feeding, and more flexed for anterior courtship licking.
source: The haustellum was more extended for ventral feeding, and more flexed for anterior courtship licking (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2G

claim: The proboscis is capable of reaching to ethologically relevant targets in different locations, making use of the head, the rostrum and the haustellum.
source: The proboscis is thus capable of reaching to ethologically relevant targets in different locations, making use of the head, the rostrum and the haustellum.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from behavioral data in Figure 2

claim: The proboscis is capable of low vs. high reaching when sucrose is placed in different locations.
source: When the sucrose was placed low or high (more ventral or more anterior, Figure 2H–J), the proboscis was indeed capable of low vs. high reaching (Figure 2K, Video 7), with decent aim (Figure 2L).
evidence: Quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2H-L and Video 7

claim: Only the haustellum showed a mean difference in angle across target positions.
source: Although individual flies could angle joints differentially to different targets (gray lines, Figure 2M–O), only the haustellum showed a mean difference across target positions (black bars, Figure 2M–O), suggesting that the haustellum can be independently controlled to aid reaching.
evidence: Statistical analysis of measurements shown in Figure 2M-O

claim: The haustellum can be independently controlled to aid reaching.
source: Although individual flies could angle joints differentially to different targets (gray lines, Figure 2M–O), only the haustellum showed a mean difference across target positions (black bars, Figure 2M–O), suggesting that the haustellum can be independently controlled to aid reaching.
evidence: Inference from statistical analysis shown in Figure 2M-O

claim: Each of the three body parts (rostrum, haustellum and head) is capable of at least some degree of independent movement.
source: Each of the three body parts (rostrum, haustellum and head) is capable of at least some degree of independent movement, since if two of the three parts were glued, the remaining part could still move (Videos 3, 4 and 8).
evidence: Demonstrated by gluing experiments shown in Videos 3, 4, and 8

claim: Reaching is guided by taste and proprioception about leg position at the time of sucrose contact, not by visual targets.
source: Reaching was guided not by a visual target (due to filming under invisible infrared light) but by contact between the waving legs and the sucrose target; the relevant sensory stimuli are therefore: 1) taste, and 2) proprioception about leg position at the time of sucrose contact.
evidence: Inference from experimental design (infrared filming) and observation of behavior

claim: A total count of 16 proboscis muscles was found in the mature adult.
source: Using 3D segmentation, we traced every muscle in the proboscis of the mature adult (Figure 3A, Video 10). We find a total count of 16 proboscis muscles.
evidence: Anatomical analysis shown in Figure 3A and Video 10

claim: Other muscles are present at eclosion, possibly to help the fly push out of the puparium, but subsequently degenerate.
source: (Other muscles are present at eclosion, possibly to help the fly push out of the puparium, but subsequently degenerate, Miller, 1950).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miller, 1950

claim: A final collection of 17 split GAL4 lines was selected, most of which target a single motor neuron type.
source: A final collection of 17 split GAL4 lines was selected, most of which target a single motor neuron type (with exceptions being one line targeting both mn11V and 12D, and three lines for mn3) (Table 1).
evidence: Result of screening and selection process, documented in Table 1

claim: One split GAL4 line targets both mn11V and 12D.
source: A final collection of 17 split GAL4 lines was selected, most of which target a single motor neuron type (with exceptions being one line targeting both mn11V and 12D, and three lines for mn3) (Table 1).
evidence: Documented in Table 1

claim: Three split GAL4 lines target mn3.
source: A final collection of 17 split GAL4 lines was selected, most of which target a single motor neuron type (with exceptions being one line targeting both mn11V and 12D, and three lines for mn3) (Table 1).
evidence: Documented in Table 1

claim: The 17 split GAL4 lines show good reproducibility of expression patterns across specimens.
source: Proboscis staining showed each line's muscle targets (Figure 4), with good reproducibility of expression patterns across specimens (Table 1).
evidence: Documented in Table 1 and shown in Figure 4

claim: The 17 split GAL4 lines are quite sparse in the CNS besides expression in proboscis motor neurons.
source: Central nervous system (CNS) staining showed that besides expression in proboscis motor neurons, these 17 were otherwise quite sparse (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), having been selected from a total of 389 combinations by CNS staining.
evidence: CNS staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: All the boutons on the relevant muscle were completely occupied by the labeled motor neurons in the split GAL4 lines.
source: To determine whether this collection was complete, we stained each line with nc82, considered a pan-synaptic marker (Wagh et al., 2006). All the boutons on the relevant muscle were indeed completely occupied by the labeled motor neurons (examples in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, N in Table 1), with two exceptions: muscle 3 is covered by separate lines (mn3M and mn3L) so was not expected to show complete occupancy, and mn10 was never labeled bilaterally in the split GAL4 line we selected (see Methods).
evidence: Synaptic marker staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and documented in Table 1

claim: The collection includes every primary motor neuron of the proboscis.
source: All other synaptic sites were occupied, and since the synaptic marker does label primary motor neuron synapses, we conclude that this collection includes every primary motor neuron.
evidence: Conclusion from complete occupancy of synaptic sites by labeled motor neurons

claim: Single motor neurons branch to many or all of the separate fibers that make up a muscle.
source: The coverage of all a muscle's synaptic sites by only one or a few motor neurons per hemisphere shows that single motor neurons must branch to many or all of the separate fibers that make up a muscle (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Inference from anatomical observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: All dendritic arbors except salivary mn13 fall into one of two regions, dorsal or ventral, which partially overlap.
source: All dendritic arbors except salivary mn13 fall into one of two regions, dorsal or ventral, which partially overlap (Figure 5B).
evidence: Anatomical analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The dorsal region is occupied by motor neurons with pharyngeal insertion sites, whereas the ventral region is generally occupied by non-pharyngeal motor neurons.
source: These divisions did not correlate with muscles found in the rostrum vs. haustellum (Table 1). Instead, with few exceptions, the dorsal region was occupied by motor neurons with pharyngeal insertion sites, whereas the ventral region was generally occupied by non-pharyngeal motor neurons (Table 1).
evidence: Anatomical correlation documented in Table 1

claim: Pharyngeal motor neurons tend to have dorsal somas and axons leaving through dorsal proboscis nerves.
source: Pharyngeal and non-pharyngeal motor neurons also tended to have dorsal and ventral somas, respectively, and axons leaving the brain through dorsal and ventral proboscis nerves ('pharyngeal' and 'compound labial' nerves, respectively, Hartenstein et al., 2018), with certain exceptions (Figure 5B, Table 1).
evidence: Anatomical correlation documented in Figure 5B and Table 1, with citation to Hartenstein et al., 2018 for nerve nomenclature

claim: Non-pharyngeal motor neurons tend to have ventral somas and axons leaving through ventral proboscis nerves.
source: Pharyngeal and non-pharyngeal motor neurons also tended to have dorsal and ventral somas, respectively, and axons leaving the brain through dorsal and ventral proboscis nerves ('pharyngeal' and 'compound labial' nerves, respectively, Hartenstein et al., 2018), with certain exceptions (Figure 5B, Table 1).
evidence: Anatomical correlation documented in Figure 5B and Table 1, with citation to Hartenstein et al., 2018 for nerve nomenclature

claim: Sweet inputs avoid the ventral arbors of the rostrum protractor's mn9.
source: Sweet inputs avoid the ventral arbors of the rostrum protractor's mn9, passing through two circular gaps to terminate more dorsally (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), consistent with their known lack of contact with mn9 (Gordon and Scott, 2009).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B, consistent with citation to Gordon and Scott, 2009

claim: Sweet inputs pass through gaps in the arbor of mn1.
source: Sweet inputs likewise pass through gaps in the arbor of mn1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), and also do not overlap with a pharyngeal neuron mn11D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Sweet inputs do not overlap with pharyngeal neuron mn11D.
source: Sweet inputs likewise pass through gaps in the arbor of mn1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), and also do not overlap with a pharyngeal neuron mn11D (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F

claim: Sweet inputs lie somewhat near the salivary mn13.
source: They do lie somewhat near the salivary mn13 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: Eye mechanosensory inputs occupy the circular gaps in motor neuron arbors.
source: We have previously shown that eye mechanosensory bristle neurons project to the ventral SEZ (Hampel et al., 2017), and now find that the glomerular-like terminals of these mechanosensory inputs occupy the circular gaps in motor neuron arbors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J, with citation to Hampel et al., 2017

claim: Motor neurons are mainly excluded from the base of the compound labial nerve where certain mechanosensory and taste inputs enter the SEZ.
source: Motor neurons are thus mainly excluded from the base of the compound labial nerve where certain mechanosensory and taste inputs enter the SEZ.
evidence: Inference from anatomical observations of motor neuron arbors and sensory input locations

claim: Bitter taste inputs do not directly overlap the retractor motor neurons.
source: Although bitter taste can cause proboscis retraction (Dethier, 1976), we find that bitter inputs do not directly overlap the retractor motor neurons (one example: Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K, with citation to Dethier, 1976 for behavioral context

claim: The main retractor motor neuron, mn1, is near peptidergic Hugin neurons.
source: The main retractor motor neuron, mn1, is near peptidergic Hugin neurons, thought to inhibit feeding initiation (Melcher and Pankratz, 2005; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1L,M, with citation to Melcher and Pankratz, 2005

claim: Hugin neurons show proximity to the salivary mn13.
source: Hugin neurons do not lie close to 9 or 11D (not shown), but do show proximity to the salivary mn13 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Computational registration shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1N

claim: Fdg shows little or no overlap with a retractor, protractor, or pharyngeal motor neuron.
source: Fdg, a pair of command-like neurons that can activate several features of the feeding motor program (Flood et al., 2013), was segmented here from a broader GAL4 line. After computationally aligning images to a common template, Fdg shows little or no overlap with a retractor, protractor, or pharyngeal motor neuron (Video 12), suggesting that there are additional interneuron layers yet to be found.
evidence: Computational registration shown in Video 12, with citation to Flood et al., 2013

claim: There are additional interneuron layers yet to be found between Fdg and motor neurons.
source: After computationally aligning images to a common template, Fdg shows little or no overlap with a retractor, protractor, or pharyngeal motor neuron (Video 12), suggesting that there are additional interneuron layers yet to be found.
evidence: Inference from lack of overlap shown in Video 12

claim: A total of eight muscles are associated with the pharynx.
source: Previously, three muscles were thought to control the pumping of food through the pharynx Flood et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998; our staining now reveals a total of eight muscles associated with the pharynx.
evidence: Anatomical analysis compared to previous work cited (Flood et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Tissot et al., 1998)

claim: Muscle 13 inserts at the junction between the salivary duct and the pharynx and is predicted to open a valve for salivation.
source: One (m13) inserts at the junction between the salivary duct and the pharynx (Figure 6A) and is predicted to open a valve for salivation.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 6A and functional prediction based on insertion site

claim: Seven muscles insert on the pharynx wall, either directly or through tendons.
source: The seven others insert on the pharynx wall (Figure 6A), either directly or through tendons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Furrows (pseudotrachea) on the labella may channel fluid to the opening of the pharynx during feeding.
source: During feeding, furrows (pseudotrachea) on the labella may channel fluid to the opening of the pharynx (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C

claim: Sequential contraction of the seven muscles attached to the pharynx would cause a traveling local dilation of the pharynx wall to move a bolus of fluid through the proboscis.
source: Because the seven muscles attached to the pharynx are arrayed along the pharynx in series, we predict that sequential contraction would cause a traveling local dilation of the pharynx wall to move a bolus of fluid through the proboscis (Video 13), acting against the elasticity of the pharynx wall rather than antagonistic muscle counterparts.
evidence: Prediction based on anatomical arrangement shown in Video 13

claim: A ring of muscles surrounding the esophagus suggests that peristaltic action takes over after food has been pumped through the pharynx.
source: After food has been pumped through the pharynx to the esophagus, a ring of muscles surrounding the esophagus suggests that peristaltic action takes over (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D

claim: Eight muscles do not insert on the pharynx and are candidates for proboscis positioning.
source: Eight other muscles were of more interest to us as they do not insert on the pharynx (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and are therefore candidates for proboscis positioning.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Activation of mn9 with CsChrimson elicited proboscis extension.
source: Now with reproducible genetic access to the bilateral pair of mn9, we activated it with CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014) and confirmed that it elicited proboscis extension (Figure 7A,K,L, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7A,K,L and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with citation to Klapoetke et al., 2014 for CsChrimson

claim: Activation of mn9 caused not only protraction of the rostrum but also extension of the haustellum.
source: We saw not only protraction of the rostrum but also extension of the haustellum (Figure 7B–C, Video 14).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7B-C and Video 14

claim: Activation of mn9 during feeding, when the proboscis is already extended, did not elicit any further extension.
source: Activation during feeding, when the proboscis is already extended, did not elicit any further extension (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E

claim: Silencing mn9 with tetanus toxin did not impair proboscis position or joint angles at rest.
source: Silencing mn9 with tetanus toxin (Sweeney et al., 1995) did not impair proboscis position or joint angles at rest (Figure 7F–H), but prevented the movement of both the rostrum and haustellum during natural feeding (Figure 7I–J, Video 14), leaving only the movement of the labella (Figure 9H, Video 14).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H, with citation to Sweeney et al., 1995 for tetanus toxin

claim: Silencing mn9 prevented the movement of both the rostrum and haustellum during natural feeding.
source: Silencing mn9 with tetanus toxin (Sweeney et al., 1995) did not impair proboscis position or joint angles at rest (Figure 7F–H), but prevented the movement of both the rostrum and haustellum during natural feeding (Figure 7I–J, Video 14), leaving only the movement of the labella (Figure 9H, Video 14).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7I-J, Figure 9H, and Video 14

claim: mn9 shows both activation and silencing phenotypes at the rostrum joint and at the haustellum joint.
source: mn9 thus shows both activation and silencing phenotypes at the rostrum joint, where its muscle is physically located, but also at the more distant haustellum joint.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from Figure 7

claim: Muscle 9 is a protractor of the rostrum, but with wider effects.
source: In sum, muscle 9 is a protractor of the rostrum, but with wider effects.
evidence: Conclusion from activation and silencing experiments

claim: Activation of mn1 retracted the proboscis into the head further than where it sits at rest by retraction of the rostrum.
source: Activation of the motor neurons for the largest of these, muscle 1, indeed retracted the proboscis into the head further than where it sits at rest (Figure 7A), by retraction of the rostrum (Figure 7B) but not the haustellum (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C

claim: Activating mn1 while the proboscis was extended for feeding triggered both retraction of the rostrum and flexion of the haustellum.
source: Activating mn1 while the proboscis was extended for feeding triggered both retraction of the rostrum and flexion of the haustellum (Figure 7D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D, Video 15).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 15

claim: Silencing mn1 impaired the retraction of the proboscis at rest.
source: Whereas activation triggered retraction, silencing mn1 showed the opposite phenotype, impairing the retraction of the proboscis at rest (Figure 7F, Video 15).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7F and Video 15

claim: Muscle 1 is a retractor, located in the rostrum but with additional effects on the haustellum.
source: In sum, muscle 1 is a retractor, located in the rostrum but with additional effects on the haustellum.
evidence: Conclusion from activation and silencing experiments

claim: mn2V activation caused rostrum retraction from rest.
source: They showed distinct roles; mn2V activation caused rostrum retraction from rest, whereas mn2D activation caused retraction from the extended position (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7B,D

claim: mn2D activation caused rostrum retraction from the extended position.
source: They showed distinct roles; mn2V activation caused rostrum retraction from rest, whereas mn2D activation caused retraction from the extended position (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7B,D

claim: Silencing mn2V caused a small impairment in how retracted the rostrum is at rest.
source: Silencing mn2V caused a small impairment in how retracted the rostrum is at rest (Figure 7G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Muscles 2D and 2V are accessory rostrum retractors.
source: In sum, muscles 2D and 2V are accessory rostrum retractors.
evidence: Conclusion from activation and silencing experiments

claim: Silencing the retractor muscles (1, 2D or 2V) did not impair the extension of the rostrum or the haustellum during feeding.
source: Silencing the retractor muscles, 1, 2D or 2V, did not impair the extension of the rostrum or the haustellum during feeding, thus we conclude that these muscles are not required for proboscis extension (Figure 7I–J), only for retraction.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 7I-J

claim: Retractor muscles (1, 2D, 2V) are not required for proboscis extension, only for retraction.
source: Silencing the retractor muscles, 1, 2D or 2V, did not impair the extension of the rostrum or the haustellum during feeding, thus we conclude that these muscles are not required for proboscis extension (Figure 7I–J), only for retraction.
evidence: Conclusion from silencing experiments shown in Figure 7I-J

claim: Muscle 9 causes rostrum protraction by anchoring on the head capsule and pulling on the free dorsal arm of the apodeme, swinging it ventrally out of the head capsule.
source: Muscle 9 causes rostrum protraction by anchoring on the head capsule and pulling on the free dorsal arm of the apodeme (via a tendon visible in Figure 6B), swinging it ventrally out of the head capsule.
evidence: Model based on anatomical observations and behavioral experiments

claim: Muscles 1, 2D and 2V control rostrum retraction by inserting on cuticle near the ventral end of the apodeme, where their contraction can draw the rostrum back into the head.
source: To counteract this protraction, retraction is controlled by muscles 1, 2D and 2V, whose dorsal ends anchor on the head capsule, and whose ventral ends insert not on the apodeme, but on cuticle near its ventral end, where their contraction can draw the rostrum back into the head (and potentially aid haustellum retraction, discussed below).
evidence: Model based on anatomical observations and behavioral experiments

claim: The role of muscles 1, 2D and 2V in rostrum retraction is supported by their decreased length in the retracted state and decreased distance between sarcomeres in the retracted state.
source: Their role in rostrum retraction is supported by their decreased length in the retracted state, their decreased distance between sarcomeres (muscle striations) in the retracted state (consistent with contraction) (Figure 7P–Q), and by the behavioral results.
evidence: Anatomical observations shown in Figure 7P-Q and behavioral results

claim: Muscle 9 controls rostrum protraction, and three muscles control retraction (1, 2D, 2V).
source: In sum, for the rostrum, we find evidence that muscle 9 controls protraction, and that three muscles control retraction (1, 2D, 2V).
evidence: Summary of anatomical and behavioral evidence

claim: The haustellum can move independently of the rostrum.
source: With the above characterization of rostrum muscles, we then sought to describe the much less well understood haustellum. Although it was affected by rostrum muscles described above, the haustellum can also move independently of the rostrum (Figure 2M–O, Video 4).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2M-O and Video 4

claim: Muscle 4 is responsible for haustellum extension.
source: We determined that the muscle responsible for haustellum extension is the previously uncharacterized muscle 4; activation of mn4 elicited haustellum extension both from the rest position (Figure 8C,K,L, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B, Video 17) and from the extended position during feeding (Figure 8E), resulting in an overall change in proboscis position (Figure 8A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8A,C,E,K,L, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B, and Video 17

claim: Activation of mn4 produced effects specific to the haustellum, not affecting the rostrum.
source: These activation phenotypes were specific to the haustellum, not affecting the rostrum (Figure 8B,D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8B,D

claim: Silencing mn4 caused a defect specific to haustellum extension during feeding.
source: Silencing instead of activating mn4 caused a defect specific to haustellum extension during feeding (Figure 8F–J, Video 17).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8F-J and Video 17

claim: Muscle 4 shows both activation and silencing phenotypes for haustellum extension.
source: Muscle 4 therefore shows both activation and silencing phenotypes for haustellum extension.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Muscle 4 may be the only muscle required for haustellum extension.
source: Since haustellum extension during feeding was virtually abolished by silencing mn4, its muscle may be the only one required for haustellum extension.
evidence: Inference from silencing experiments

claim: Muscle 3 controls haustellum flexion.
source: In opposition to extension, we find that haustellum flexion is controlled by muscle 3.
evidence: Conclusion from experiments described in subsequent text

claim: mn3M&1, mn3M&7 and mn3L all triggered haustellum flexion during feeding.
source: Activating mn3 demonstrated that it acts as a haustellum flexor. mn3M&1, mn3M&7 and mn3L all triggered haustellum flexion during feeding (Figure 8E,M,N, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–D, Video 18).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8E,M,N, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-D, and Video 18

claim: Muscle 3 is responsible for haustellum flexion, not the contaminating cell types mn1 or mn7.
source: Although the contaminating cell type mn1 does so as well (Figure 7E), the contaminating mn7 does not (Figure 9N), suggesting that muscle 3 is responsible.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental results shown in Figure 7E and Figure 9N

claim: All mn3 lines triggered additional proboscis retraction from the resting proboscis position.
source: From the resting proboscis position, all mn3 lines could trigger additional proboscis retraction (Figure 8A), although that could not be attributed to a specific joint (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8A-C

claim: mn3M&1 and mn3M&7 both impaired proboscis retraction at rest.
source: In silencing experiments, mn3M&1 and mn3M&7 both impaired proboscis retraction at rest (Figure 8F, Video 18).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 8F and Video 18

claim: Muscle 3 is responsible for impaired proboscis retraction at rest, not the contaminating cell types mn1 or mn7.
source: Although the contaminating cell type mn1 does so as well (Figure 7F), the contaminating mn7 does not (Figure 9O), suggesting that muscle 3 is responsible.
evidence: Inference from comparison of experimental results shown in Figure 7F and Figure 9O

claim: Muscle 3 is a haustellum flexor.
source: In sum, by examining three different lines for mn3, we conclude that muscle 3 is a haustellum flexor.
evidence: Conclusion from activation and silencing experiments with multiple lines

claim: Haustellum extension correlates with the rotation of a Y-shaped apodeme found within the joint.
source: Combining these behavioral results with anatomical results, we propose a model of the action of the haustellum. Imaging the haustellum in different positions (Figure 8O–P) shows that its extension correlates with the rotation of a Y-shaped apodeme found within the joint.
evidence: Anatomical observations shown in Figure 8O-P

claim: Muscle 4 originates from a rigid part of the rostrum and inserts upon the free dorsal arm of the Y-shaped apodeme.
source: We propose that a muscle pulling against the free dorsal arm could rotate the haustellum anteriorly away from the rostrum. Indeed, we found that muscle 4 originates from a rigid part of the rostrum and inserts upon the free dorsal arm of the Y, where its contraction would cause rotation of the apodeme and thus haustellum extension.
evidence: Anatomical observation

claim: Muscle 4 contraction causes rotation of the apodeme and thus haustellum extension.
source: Indeed, we found that muscle 4 originates from a rigid part of the rostrum and inserts upon the free dorsal arm of the Y, where its contraction would cause rotation of the apodeme and thus haustellum extension. Behavioral experiments above did show that muscle 4 was a haustellum extensor.
evidence: Model based on anatomical observations and confirmed by behavioral experiments

claim: Muscle 2V inserts upon the anterior arm of the Y-shaped apodeme where it could rotate the apodeme dorsally.
source: Another muscle, 2V, inserts upon the anterior arm (Figure 8O–P) where it could rotate the apodeme back in the other direction, dorsally.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 8O-P

claim: Muscle 3 is ideally located to act as a haustellum flexor, coming from the anterior rostrum and crossing the joint with the haustellum.
source: Instead, another muscle, 3, was ideally located to act as a flexor (Figure 8O–P); coming from the anterior rostrum, it crosses the joint with the haustellum so that it could pull on the haustellum to fold it in towards the rostrum. In behavioral experiments (above), muscle 3 indeed triggered haustellum flexion.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 8O-P and confirmed by behavioral experiments

claim: Muscle 4 controls haustellum extension and muscle 3 (possibly also 2V) controls flexion.
source: In sum, we find evidence that muscle 4 controls haustellum extension and that muscle 3 (possibly also 2V) controls flexion.
evidence: Summary of anatomical and behavioral evidence

claim: Muscle 4 appears more contracted when the haustellum is more extended, based on distances between sarcomeres.
source: Indeed, based on distances between sarcomeres (Figure 8O–P), muscle 4 appears more contracted when the haustellum is more extended, and 2V and 3 appear more contracted when the haustellum is more flexed.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 8O-P

claim: Muscles 2V and 3 appear more contracted when the haustellum is more flexed, based on distances between sarcomeres.
source: Indeed, based on distances between sarcomeres (Figure 8O–P), muscle 4 appears more contracted when the haustellum is more extended, and 2V and 3 appear more contracted when the haustellum is more flexed.
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figure 8O-P

claim: Muscles 6 and 7 insert upon the lip-like labella.
source: The remaining two muscles (6 and 7) of the eight tested for roles in proboscis positioning were both found to insert upon on the lip-like labella (Figures 6B and 9A–C).
evidence: Anatomical observation shown in Figures 6B and 9A-C

claim: Muscle 6 shows both activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar extension.
source: Muscle 6 shows both activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar extension (Figure 9F,H, Video 19).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 9F,H and Video 19

claim: Muscle 7 shows activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar abduction.
source: Muscle 7 shows activation and silencing phenotypes for labellar abduction (the opening of the two lobes, Figure 9G,I, Video 20).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 9G,I and Video 20

claim: mn7 activation induced labellar extension, but this may be a side effect of abduction.
source: Although mn7 activation also induced labellar extension (Figure 9F), that may be a side effect of abduction; muscle 7 showed no effect on labellar extension when silenced (Figure 9H).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 9F,H and inference from comparison

claim: Muscle 6 and 7 are the only muscles that showed labellar phenotypes.
source: Muscle 6 and 7 are therefore the only muscles that showed labellar phenotypes.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: All eight of the muscles predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning indeed showed positioning phenotypes.
source: To summarize the behavioral results, all eight of the muscles predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning (based on the location of their insertion sites) indeed showed positioning phenotypes; six control reaching movements and two control the labella.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Six muscles control reaching movements and two control the labella.
source: To summarize the behavioral results, all eight of the muscles predicted to be involved in proboscis positioning (based on the location of their insertion sites) indeed showed positioning phenotypes; six control reaching movements and two control the labella.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: Most of the findings about muscle functions were not previously known or differed from previous work.
source: Most of these findings (Table 3) were not previously known or, in some cases, differed from previous work (Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previous work cited (Schwarz et al., 2017), documented in Table 3

claim: This work provides the first comprehensive, genetically reproducible control of every primary motor neuron type for an appendage.
source: Building on previous studies in insects that have analyzed motor neurons in body parts such as the legs and proboscis (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012; Maniates-Selvin et al., 2020; Rajashekhar and Singh, 1994; Schwarz et al., 2017; Trimarchi and Schneiderman, 1994), we now provide the first comprehensive, genetically reproducible control of every primary motor neuron type for an appendage.
evidence: Comparison with previous work cited and summary of current work

claim: The neurons of this collection are considered to be primary excitatory motor neurons.
source: We consider the neurons of this collection to be primary excitatory motor neurons, as they do not resemble known modulatory motor neurons in adult flies, which are characterized by thin axons and small boutons on multiple muscles (Rivlin et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison with known modulatory motor neurons cited (Rivlin et al., 2004)

claim: The neurons of this collection do not resemble inhibitory motor neurons found in several arthropods.
source: Likewise, they do not resemble inhibitory motor neurons found in several arthropods, which mostly innervate multiple muscles (Wolf, 2014).
evidence: Comparison with known inhibitory motor neurons cited (Wolf, 2014)

claim: Both mn9 and mn1 are located near the rostrum but showed phenotypic effects on the haustellum as well.
source: We discover unexpected complexity of phenotypes from rostrum motor neurons. Both mn9 and mn1 are located near the rostrum, not in a position to control the haustellum directly, yet showed phenotypic effects on the haustellum as well.
evidence: Summary of experimental results

claim: The phenotypic effects of mn9 and mn1 on the haustellum may represent examples of biomechanical coupling.
source: These may represent examples of biomechanical coupling.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: Optogenetically forcing the movement of one body part may cause a fly to move another in response, even if the activated motor neuron is not directly involved.
source: We were struck by how common 'side effects' like this were – another example is that, although mn7 is responsible for labellar abduction (with both activation and silencing phenotypes), its activation also triggers labellar extension. We speculate that optogenetically forcing the movement of one body part may cause a fly to move another in response, even if the activated motor neuron is not directly involved in the latter at all, or that forced movement about a joint may cause afferent feedback that leads to activation of other motor neurons.
evidence: Speculation based on observed side effects

claim: Forced movement about a joint may cause afferent feedback that leads to activation of other motor neurons.
source: We speculate that optogenetically forcing the movement of one body part may cause a fly to move another in response, even if the activated motor neuron is not directly involved in the latter at all, or that forced movement about a joint may cause afferent feedback that leads to activation of other motor neurons.
evidence: Speculation based on observed side effects

claim: Intrinsic biomechanical properties, such as passive joint forces, provide non-neural aid during motor responses to mechanical perturbations in insect legs during locomotion.
source: Intrinsic biomechanical properties, such as passive joint forces, are also known to provide non-neural (and rapid) aid during motor responses to mechanical perturbations, for example in cockroach, locust and stick insect legs during locomotion (Ache and Matheson, 2013; Jindrich and Full, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ache and Matheson, 2013; Jindrich and Full, 2002

claim: Combining activation, silencing, and insertion site data allows derivation of interpretations of muscle roles.
source: By incorporating activation, silencing, and insertion site data, we derive interpretations of muscle roles (Table 3) that differ in several respects from those of a previous work based mainly on activation (Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: Methodological approach and comparison with previous work cited (Schwarz et al., 2017)

claim: Several muscles were innervated by only a single primary motor neuron.
source: Several muscles were innervated by only a single primary motor neuron, but in the case where two were present, it is possible that they control slow twitch and fast twitch fibers, as found in both the fly (Azevedo et al., 2019) and in mammalian muscle, to fine-tune the strength of a muscle response.
evidence: Observation from anatomical analysis, with citation to Azevedo et al., 2019 for comparison

claim: When two primary motor neurons are present for a muscle, they may control slow twitch and fast twitch fibers to fine-tune the strength of a muscle response.
source: Several muscles were innervated by only a single primary motor neuron, but in the case where two were present, it is possible that they control slow twitch and fast twitch fibers, as found in both the fly (Azevedo et al., 2019) and in mammalian muscle, to fine-tune the strength of a muscle response.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison with known mechanisms cited (Azevedo et al., 2019)

claim: The dramatic numerical simplicity of only one or two primary motor neurons per muscle in flies presents an experimental advantage for future circuit studies.
source: Regardless, the dramatic numerical simplicity of only one or two primary motor neurons per muscle in flies presents an experimental advantage for future circuit studies.
evidence: Inference from anatomical observations

claim: The proboscis has a varied repertoire of movements in feeding and courtship.
source: Given that the proboscis has a varied repertoire of movements in feeding and courtship (Manzo et al., 2012; McKellar et al., 2019), one exciting avenue would be to decipher the circuit logic of how different movements with multiple behavioral functions can arise from these few motor neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Manzo et al., 2012; McKellar et al., 2019

claim: Activation and inactivation experiments of individual proboscis motor neuron types support a model of separable control, enabling articulated movements that allow flexibility.
source: Activation and inactivation experiments of individual proboscis motor neuron types support a model of separable control, enabling articulated movements that allow flexibility.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental results

claim: Humans show sophisticated, learned arm and hand movements.
source: Directed reaching occurs in different forms: humans show sophisticated, learned arm and hand movements (Parker, 1974), yet newborns show a more basic, innate form of intentional reaching (Bower et al., 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parker, 1974

claim: Newborns show a more basic, innate form of intentional reaching.
source: Directed reaching occurs in different forms: humans show sophisticated, learned arm and hand movements (Parker, 1974), yet newborns show a more basic, innate form of intentional reaching (Bower et al., 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bower et al., 1970

claim: Forms of reaching exist in smaller animals such as rodents and cephalopods.
source: Forms of reaching exist in smaller animals such as rodents and cephalopods (Gutnick et al., 2011; Peterson, 1934).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gutnick et al., 2011; Peterson, 1934

claim: Proboscis reaching in flies could present a new model for understanding the neural circuit basis of goal-directed movement.
source: We propose that proboscis reaching in flies could present a new model for understanding the neural circuit basis of goal-directed movement.
evidence: Proposal based on the work presented

claim: Drosophila has rich behavior, a smaller nervous system, and powerful genetic tools.
source: Drosophila has rich behavior, a smaller nervous system, and powerful genetic tools.
evidence: General knowledge about Drosophila as a model system

claim: A whole-brain synaptic connectome is underway for Drosophila.
source: Additionally, a whole-brain synaptic connectome is underway (see flywire.ai, based on the images of Zheng et al., 2017) that can help map how diverse interneurons may converge upon this small set of motor neurons to produce a repertoire of flexible motor behaviors from a single appendage.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2017
